lessons.title: Assessing the problem-animal situation
lessons.html:
The scale of the problem

Predation and crop damage by wild and feral animals cost South African farmers a great deal each year. Black-backed jackal and caracal kill sheep, goats and calves in the Karoo, Free State and Eastern Cape. Baboons, vervet monkeys, bushpigs and porcupines damage crops, orchards and irrigation lines. Feral and stray dogs can kill dozens of sheep in one night. At management level, problem-animal control is not just about killing animals; it is a planned, legal and cost-effective program that reduces losses over the long term.

Identify the real culprit

Many losses are wrongly blamed on predators. Before acting, confirm the cause.

  • Examine carcasses: bite position, bruising under the skin, feeding pattern and tracks. Jackal often bite at the throat; caracal often bite at the throat or nape and may feed from the inside of the hindleg; dogs typically cause many scattered wounds. Confirm with a trained person, because signs overlap.
  • Distinguish predation from scavenging: an animal that died of disease or cold and was later eaten shows no bleeding or bruising at the bite.
  • Use tracks, scat, camera traps and herder reports.

Quantify the loss

Keep a loss register: date, camp, species and class of livestock, cause, evidence and value in rand. Compare the cost of losses with the cost of control. A program that costs R80 000 a year to save R20 000 of stock is not sound management, unless it also prevents a growing problem.

Understand the ecology

Removing predators can create a vacuum that is quickly filled by young dispersing animals, sometimes causing higher losses. Predators also control rodents, hares and dassies that compete for grazing. Effective programs focus on the individual damage-causing animal and on protecting livestock, not on wiping out a species.

lessons.title: Legal and ethical framework
lessons.html:
Know the law before you act

Wild animals are protected by national and provincial legislation. The National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 and the provincial nature conservation laws control hunting, trapping, poisoning and the handling of protected species. Many species, including leopard, brown hyena, cheetah and honey badger, are protected and may not be killed without a permit. Even where a species such as jackal may be controlled by landowners, the methods are regulated.

Practical rules for managers

  • Contact your provincial conservation authority before starting a control program, and obtain written permits where required.
  • Many methods are prohibited or restricted, for example certain poisons, gin traps and hunting at night with lights. Check what is legal in your province; rules differ.
  • Only use registered products for any chemical control, exactly according to the label, under Act 36 of 1947. Poisons kill non-target species, pets and birds of prey, and can harm people.
  • Firearms may be used only by licensed, competent people under the Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 forbids causing unnecessary suffering; traps must be checked often and any captured animal dealt with humanely.

Ethics and reputation

Buyers and the public increasingly expect wildlife-friendly farming. Indiscriminate killing can damage the farm's reputation and its market access. Keep records of every animal removed, the method, the location and the permit used. Train staff and contractors in the rules, and take responsibility as the manager for their actions.

Working with neighbours

Predators cross fences. Area-wide cooperation through farmers' associations, shared information and coordinated action usually works better than a single farm acting alone.

lessons.title: Designing an integrated control program
lessons.html:
Integrated control

The best programs combine several methods and put prevention first. Lethal control is a last step, aimed at the specific animal causing damage.

ApproachExamples
HusbandryKraaling sheep at night, lambing in camps near the homestead, shorter lambing seasons, removing carcasses
GuardingLivestock guarding dogs such as Anatolian shepherds, alpacas or donkeys, herders
Physical barriersJackal-proof and electrified fencing, protective collars on lambs
DeterrentsLights, noise devices, changing their position often
Selective removalCage traps, legal trapping or shooting of the identified problem animal by a competent person

Crop damage

For baboons and monkeys: remove food sources, keep rubbish secure, use trained monitors and electrified fencing. For bushpigs and porcupines: well-maintained fencing with buried wire or electric strands. Consult the provincial authority for persistent problems.

Safety

Cornered predators, baboons and bushpigs can cause serious injury. Never approach a trapped animal without training. Handle firearms only if licensed, and never shoot towards roads, homes or where people work. Wear gloves when handling carcasses to avoid disease.

Monitor and review

Set targets, for example reducing lamb losses from 8% to 3%. Review the loss register each season, calculate cost per animal saved and adjust the program.

Key points

  • Confirm the real cause of loss before acting, using carcass signs and evidence.
  • Know and follow national and provincial wildlife law; get permits where required.
  • Put prevention first: kraaling, guard animals, fencing and herding.
  • Target only the specific damage-causing animal, humanely and legally.
  • Keep a loss register and measure cost against benefit.
